We developed HOMED (Hierarchically Optimized Methylation Deconvolution), a framework that integrates cell-type hierarchy, single-cell RNA sequencing-guided deconvolution, and paired bulk RNA-seq/DNAm data for CpG signature optimization. Across multiple simulated and real heterogeneous tissue datasets, HOMED achieved a 68% higher mean Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) and 60% lower mean root mean squared error (RMSE), compared to other scRNA-seq-guided or single-cell DNA methylation-based DNAm deconvolution methods. Moreover, application of HOMED to a smoking-exposed placenta DNA methylation cohort revealed significant shifts in cell-type compositions in endothelial, nRBC, stromal, and villous trophoblast proportions. Adjusting for these compositional differences reduced inflated smoking-associated CpGs by nearly three folds, and doubled the number of enriched pathways with known associations to smoking. In summary, HOMED is an accurate and practical method to infer cell-type proportions from bulk DNA methylation data.

papers.t: A unique intestinal epithelial cell that expresses canonical lymphoid genes.
papers.ab: Enterocytes and intestinal secretory cells harbor innate immunity. However, certain transcriptional programs -even beyond rearranged T- and B-cell receptor genes- are considered the exclusive purview of adaptive immune cells, including abundant and diverse intestinal intra-epithelial lymphocytes (IELs). Here, we identify and characterize columnar intestinal secretory cells that co-express classic epithelial and lymphoid genes, including Ptprc, Cd3e, Cd8a, and Gzma/b but not T- or B-cell receptors. These previously unrecognized epithelium-derived lymphoid-like cells (EDLCs) differ from any known resident cell type, including IELs or tuft cells. Rare in healthy mouse and human intestines, their numbers increase upon IL-25 stimulation or IL-10 receptor deficiency in vivo and upon IL-13 stimulation in vitro. EDLC chromatin is uniquely accessible at thousands of cis-elements, including lymphoid and epithelial loci. These findings reveal a transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct intestinal epithelial derivative that expresses prominent lymphoid character.

papers.t: Single-Nucleus Profiling Reveals Neuronal Metabolic Collapse During the Transition to Alzheimer's Disease Dementia.
papers.ab: Current Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathological metrics, including Thal phasing, and Braak staging, often do not accurately predict cognitive status: many cognitively resilient individuals have substantial pathological burdens, whereas some patients with dementia show minimal classical AD pathology. Here, we addressed this discrepancy by investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying AD dementia using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and single-nucleus multiome datasets. To eliminate cross-modality scaling artifacts and compositional biases inherent in neurodegenerative tissues, we normalized the datasets using our novel framework, bypassing scaling issues of conventional methods that may obscure critical biological signals of interest. We identified neuron-specific suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and their upstream mitochondrial biogenesis signaling (MBS) as primary drivers of clinical dementia. By integrating multi-omic quantitative trait loci, genome-wide association studies, and epigenomic profiles, we delineated genetic and epigenetic changes underlying MBS suppression. This study provides a systematic genomic framework for understanding the mechanisms of cognitive resilience.

papers.t: A MultiOmics time-resolved systems map of gene regulation in Toxoplasma gondii.
papers.ab: Understanding how T. gondii builds an invasion-competent cell has been limited by its rapid, asynchronous division cycle, incomplete gene function annotation, and studies that have examined one regulator or complex at a time. Here, we placed acute perturbation of 21 transcriptional and epigenetic factors, promoter occupancy, chromatin accessibility, and molecular validation on a common single-cell clock. The resulting consensus map links the lytic-cycle programs to candidate activating and repressive inputs, organizes genes into 108 co-regulated communities, and nominates regulatory partnerships that would not have emerged from any single data type. The work bridges three longstanding gaps: it resolves perturbation responses in cell-cycle time, distinguishes promoter occupancy from perturbation-linked regulation, and turns a large multidimensional dataset into an experimentally navigable map. We indeed confirmed known factor interactions such as MORC/HDAC3, and recovered combinations such as the Cdc5/SNIP1 and DMAP1/EPL1 as coregulatory nodes (that in other systems have been described to cooperate). Furthermore, we discovered a novel apicomplexan specific combination of AAF1/AP2XI-5 that provides mechanistic insights of the unique AP2 transcription factor family.

papers.t: Influence of the male germline on B chromosome transmission in D. melanogaster.
papers.ab: Selfish genetic elements that bias their inheritance to the detriment to their host are in an evolutionary arms race with host-derived suppressors that neutralize the spread of these elements. The supernumerary B chromosomes recently found in a mutant Drosophila melanogaster laboratory stock are subject to drive (>50% transmission) when passed through the female germline, but through the male germline they experience the opposite of drive, a phenomenon referred to as drag (<50% transmission). Here we show that males from this mutant stock do not have fertility defects, excluding the possibility that sperm carrying more B chromosomes are inviable. Though we revealed irregularities in the germline stem cell (GSC) niche, we show that other aspects of GSCs activity is normal: there is no delay in their mitoses and the B chromosomes appear to be symmetrically segregated during the GSC divisions, suggesting that the asymmetry of these divisions is not likely the source of B chromosome drag. Together, this work lays the foundation for future studies into the mechanism of paternal B chromosome drag in D. melanogaster , which is poised to significantly advance on our understanding of how various genetic and developmental contexts promote disparate chromosome behavior.

papers.t: Modeling of human MLH1 and MLH3 variants in mice reveals novel functions of MutLγ in meiotic DNA repair and the ovarian reserve.
papers.ab: The mismatch repair proteins MLH1 and MLH3 form the MutLγ complex that is essential for >90% of meiotic crossovers (CO) in mice. Although deletion of either gene causes infertility, we previously found that mouse models of certain human MLH1/3 missense variants caused elevated aneuploidy and progressive loss of female fecundity despite having a normal ovarian reserve. Here, we report that additional missense and null alleles caused significant pre-pubertal follicle loss independent of alterations to meiotic CO levels. Deletion of the DNA damage checkpoint kinase Chek2 (Chk2) partially rescued the oocyte pool of Mlh1- and Mlh3 -deficient mice, indicating that defects in meiotic prophase I triggered oocyte elimination. In spermatocytes, both missense and null alleles caused abnormal γH2AX 'flares' on autosomes during late pachynema and diplonema, extending into chromatin loops from the synaptonemal complex. These flares frequently contained unusually large foci of the ssDNA binding protein RPA as well as DNA end processing factors including CtIP, RAD50 and BLM, consistent with abnormal and extensive DNA resection. The results reveal a previously unrecognized meiotic function of MutLγ in preventing DNA hyper-resection of spontaneous DNA breaks or of persistent recombination intermediates in late prophase I. Together with our previous studies, the results show that MLH1/3 variants can impair fertility through at least three mechanistically distinct routes: severe crossover loss sufficient to activate the metaphase I spindle assembly checkpoint; subthreshold crossover defects that increase aneuploidy and embryo loss; and abnormal late-prophase DNA processing that activates a CHEK2-dependent oocyte quality-control pathway and depletes the ovarian reserve, causing primary ovarian insufficiency (POI). Thus, MutLγ has broader roles in maintaining meiotic genome integrity than can be explained by crossover formation alone.

papers.t: LongVerse: verified AI agents for Nanopore and PacBio DNA methylation analysis.
papers.ab: AI agents now run sequencing pipelines, but their outputs are checked by rubrics or language-model judges, not against an independent measurement. LongVerse turns one English sentence into haplotype-resolved DNA methylation from Nanopore or PacBio reads, through agents that read the data, supply arguments to a pinned pipeline and never write code. On HG002, a healthy reference genome, agent and human expert produced byte-identical calls (r = 1.000) that agreed with bisulfite sequencing (r = 0.943, 0.884), at $0.12 to $0.54 of conversation per run. A consensus agent that admits any per-site caller reduced error 10.7 percent against the best published caller.

papers.t: cBAF drives AR-V7 expression through regulation of transcriptional termination in castration-resistant prostate cancer.
papers.ab: UNLABELLED: The androgen receptor splice variant AR-V7 drives resistance to androgen receptor-targeted therapies in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), but the mechanisms governing its expression remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the canonical BAF (cBAF) chromatin remodeling complex as a selective regulator of AR-V7 expression. Pharmacologic and genetic disruption of cBAF reduced AR-V7 levels, suppressed AR-V7-dependent transcriptional programs, and impaired CRPC cell proliferation. Mechanistically, cBAF binds an intronic regulatory element downstream of AR cryptic exon 3, where it maintains chromatin accessibility, enhancer activity, and promoter-enhancer looping. cBAF loss decreases recruitment of transcription termination machinery, reduces RNA polymerase II Thr4 phosphorylation, and promotes transcriptional readthrough beyond the AR-V7 polyadenylation site. POINT-seq revealed that cBAF-dependent transcriptional termination is required for AR-V7 biogenesis and regulates termination at a subset of genes genome-wide. Together, these findings uncover a role for cBAF in chromatin-mediated control of transcriptional termination and establish this mechanism as a critical determinant of AR-V7 expression. KEY FINDINGS: cBAF is the only SWI/SNF subcomplex required for AR-V7 expression and function.AR-V7 transcription requires cBAF-promoted premature transcriptional termination in addition to alternative splicing.cBAF maintains an intronic enhancer-like regulatory element through chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac, and chromatin looping.cBAF broadly influences RNA polymerase II termination dynamics, revealing a previously unrecognized role in transcriptional termination.

papers.t: Early-onset spontaneous murine mammary tumors show increased lymphocyte representation and reduced MHC antigen presentation.
papers.ab: SIMPLE SUMMARY: Not all breast tumors behave the same way, and part of the reason may be inherited rather than caused by the tumor itself. Using mice that carry the same cancer-causing HER2/neu gene but differ in genetic background, we found that introduction of the PWK/PhJ genetic background was associated with tumors that appeared about a month earlier. These early tumors contained a larger proportion of immune cells, including T and B cells, but the T-cell population showed reduced expression of genes associated with cytotoxic activity. At the same time, the tumors had lower levels of proteins and genes that let the immune system recognize tumor cells, alongside higher levels of structural proteins that can make tissue stiffer and easier for cancer to invade. These findings suggest that genetic background shapes not only how quickly breast tumors arise but also how well the immune system can recognize them, a distinction that may matter for future immune-based treatments. BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Genetic background modifies cancer risk and phenotype in humans, but its influence on the tumor immune microenvironment and antigen-presentation machinery in ErbB2 (HER2/neu)-driven breast cancer is not well defined. We used a genetically diverse mouse cross to test whether the wild-derived PWK/PhJ background alters immune infiltration and antigen presentation in a NeuT model of HER2/neu-positive breast cancer. METHODS: Previously, quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping using Diversity Outbred mice and r/qtl2 identified candidate loci driving tumor onset and growth. The wild-derived PWK/PhJ genetic background was predicted to harbor genes that regulated early onset of HER2/neu-driven tumors. BALB NeuT and (BALBxPWK) F1 NeuT female mice were monitored twice weekly for spontaneous mammary tumor onset and growth. Tumor immune composition was profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. Protein abundance was measured by data-independent acquisition proteomics in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue (n=5 per genotype). Single-nucleus multiome (RNA + ATAC), bulk RNA-seq, and H3K27ac datasets from the same strain comparison were analyzed for focused MHC II cross-layer analyses. RESULTS: As predicted, (BALBxPWK) F1 NeuT mice developed tumors significantly earlier than the parental BALB NeuT mice (10 vs. 14-15 weeks of age; p < 0.0001). In the scRNA-seq dataset, F1 tumors showed greater representation of Cd3e -expressing T cells and a Cd79a -expressing B-cell population not detected in BALB NeuT tumors, and a distinct neutrophil cluster; F1 T cells also showed lower expression of the cytotoxicity-associated genes Tox, Ltk, Nkg7 , and Gzmb relative to BALB NeuT tumor-infiltrating T cells. Proteomics identified 46 differentially abundant proteins (25 higher, 21 lower in F1), with coordinate down-regulation of Stat1, Tapbp, Parp9 , and Dtx3l alongside MHC class I and II proteins and up-regulation of extracellular-matrix and elastic-fiber proteins. Focused cross-layer analysis showed lower whole-tumor expression of a Stat1 /MHC II-associated gene set together with reduced epithelial chromatin accessibility at selected regions near Cd74 and H2-Aa . CONCLUSIONS: The PWK/PhJ genetic background is associated with earlier HER2-driven tumor onset, greater lymphocyte representation, and reduced activity of a STAT1-associated antigen-presentation program despite similar post-onset tumor growth kinetics.

papers.t: Histone modifications define distinct nucleosome positions in cell-free DNA.
papers.ab: Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentation patterns reflect nucleosome positioning. We asked whether variation in nucleosome positions in cfDNA can reveal chromatin states and associated histone modifications. Using cell-free chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (cfChIP-seq) in plasma from patients with prostate cancer, we identified 35,120 modification-associated positions (MAPs), loci where nucleosomes bearing active (H3K4me2) and repressive (H3K9me3) histone marks occupy reproducibly offset positions. These offsets recurred across histone marks, an independent cfChIP-seq cohort, and nuclease-digested chromatin from cell lines. MAPs were enriched in transcribed genes but depleted near transcription start sites and CTCF-binding sites where nucleosome positioning is constrained. Across 2,535 cfDNA sequencing datasets, nucleosome protection at a subset of MAPs correlated with tumor fraction (TF), reflecting differences in histone modification status between cancer-derived and non-malignant chromatin. In targeted sequencing panels, a 50-MAP model using fragments from < 0.001% of the genome distinguished samples with tumor fractions ≥3% vs 0% (AUCs = 0.91-0.96 across prostate, breast, and lung cancers) and outperformed a state-of-the-art fragmentomics-based tumor fraction predictor. MAP-derived estimates correlated with reference TFs (r = 0.89) and longitudinal changes in TF (r = 0.91). MAP protection at ASCL1 binding sites identified neuroendocrine transformation of prostate cancer from cfDNA. These findings establish histone-modification-associated nucleosome positioning as a mutation-independent readout of tumor fraction and cancer state from routine cfDNA sequencing.

papers.t: Engineered Tn5 Variants Enhance CUT&Tag Fidelity for Transcription Factors.
papers.ab: The CUT&Tag method performs exceptionally well for profiling histone modifications, but mapping sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) is complicated by intrinsic Tn5 activity at accessible DNA, and the high-salt washes used to suppress this activity can destabilize TF-chromatin interactions. We engineered the Tn5 DNA-binding channel to attenuate target-DNA engagement by replacing individual positively charged amino acids with neutral amino acids. We identified a "Goldilocks" variant (K160A) with intermediate attenuation that improved recovery of GATA2 motif-containing sites under low-salt CUT&Tag and KCl-based DynaTag conditions. A second variant (K249A) had improved performance for profiling CTCF over less accessible sites characterized by sharply focused short-fragment enrichment. By comparing the K160A and K249A variants, this TF-CUT&Tag assay provides a physical readout of the local chromatin environment at TF binding sites. Applying K160A TF-CUT&Tag to pluripotency-associated TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells increased recovery across their genomic binding landscapes while preserving factor-specific motif architectures. During skeletal muscle differentiation, TF-CUT&Tag improved recovery of MyoG and Pax7 occupancy relative to standard CUT&Tag, revealing strongly motif-enriched MyoG binding and a shift in Pax7 binding from CpG-rich promoters in progenitors toward Pax7 motif-enriched sites during differentiation. Together, these results show that TF-CUT&Tag captures distinct modes of TF- chromatin interaction, including motif-directed binding sites and more salt-sensitive sites that may depend on lower-affinity DNA recognition or protein-protein interactions and are difficult to predict from DNA sequence alone.

papers.t: Histone modifications directly modulate transcription factor binding to nucleosomes.
papers.ab: Transcription factors (TFs) that can recognize specific DNA sequences within nucleosomes play key roles in regulating cell fate transitions, but what regulates their condition-dependent binding to nucleosomes remains poorly understood. Here, we determined the direct effects of H3K27ac, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 on binding by 7 human TFs to a highly diverse library of nucleosomes. We found that these marks influence the preference of FOXA1 and PAX7 to bind as monomers versus dimers to nucleosomes. Furthermore, H3K27ac impairs TF binding at internal regions of nucleosomes, enhancing end-binding preferences, for most of the assayed TFs. Our results suggest that histone marks represent an additional layer of cis-regulatory encoding that directly regulates TF interactions with nucleosomal binding sites.

papers.t: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis.
papers.ab: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1-3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4-7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

papers.t: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice.
papers.ab: Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1-3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

papers.t: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia.
papers.ab: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2+ STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

papers.t: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
papers.ab: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.t: Stepping (hi)stones: Charting a single-cell multiomic path toward understanding the human brain.
papers.ab: In this issue of Cell, two single-cell multiomic atlases jointly profile transcription and histone modifications across different regions of the adult human brain, revealing cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, developmental epigenetic memory, and improved interpretation of neurological variants. These studies establish a framework for understanding human brain cell identity, evolution, and pathology.

papers.t: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
papers.ab: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

papers.t: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain.
papers.ab: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

papers.t: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
papers.ab: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

papers.t: Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging.
papers.ab: Implantation remains the most inaccessible stage of mammalian development. Consequently, we know remarkably little about how the embryo coordinates the cellular transitions that establish the body plan and initiate placental formation, despite this being the period when most pregnancies are lost. Here we combine single-cell transcriptomics, live imaging and functional experiments to define these transitions at cellular resolution. Our results identify an intermediate state bridging naive and primed pluripotency in the embryonic lineage, trace anterior-posterior axis specification origins in the extraembryonic endoderm, and reveal trophectoderm bifurcation into distinct placental progenitors. Strikingly, we find that the placenta arises from two sources: the classically recognized polar trophectoderm and a previously unrecognized population of mural trophectoderm that migrates from the polar-mural border. Human mural trophectoderm shows similar region-specific behaviour and may include invasive-trophoblast-biased progenitors. These findings open new directions for improving stem-cell-derived embryo models and uncovering the early determinants of pregnancy success.

papers.t: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells.
papers.ab: Horizontal gene transfer drives rapid evolutionary innovation, yet well-substantiated cases are largely confined to prokaryotes. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer remains exceptionally rare, and direct genome-scale demonstrations are absent. Here, inspired by endosymbiotic genome acquisition, we show that mammalian cells can initiate genome-scale horizontal gene transfer through phagocytic uptake of intact algal cells, albeit at a much lower frequency than cell fusion. Live-cell imaging captures the early nuclear appearance of transferred algal DNA after fusion, while genome sequencing and cytogenetic analyses reveal stable retention of chromosome-scale algal DNA in mammalian cells. Hybrid cells maintain more than 16 Mb of algal DNA, including intact chromosomes, as telomere-linked structures that persist for 95 generations without selection. Transferred algal DNA shows a progressive increase in DNA methylation together with enrichment of repressive histone modifications, forming heterochromatic domains that physically associate with host chromosomes. Notably, mammalian cells deficient in a de novo DNA methyltransferase show reduced stable establishment and retention of transferred algal DNA, supporting a gatekeeping role for DNA methylation in the stable accommodation of foreign genomes. Our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism that contributes to the stable accommodation of large-scale foreign DNA between distantly related eukaryotes.

papers.t: Discrete subdomains establish epigenetic diversity in subtelomeric heterochromatin in fission yeast.
papers.ab: Subtelomeres are imperfect repeats adjacent to telomeres that are transcriptionally repressed by heterochromatin. Although essential for genome integrity, their repetitive nature has thwarted dissection of local heterochromatin assembly and maintenance mechanisms. By engineering fission yeast strains carrying fluorescent reporters at a single subtelomere, we uncovered distinct subdomains. These subdomains have different silencing requirements: telomere-proximal regions rely on canonical shelterin- or RNAi-dependent nucleation pathways, whereas telomere-distal regions involve nucleosome remodelers, histone chaperones, and boundary-associated factors. Subdomains also exhibit discrete epigenetic states emerging both at homologous loci on different chromosome arms and along the same subtelomeric sequence. We document these epigenetic states using multi-generational live imaging and targeted perturbations. These analyses show that subtelomeric subdomains display position-specific, clonally variable silencing across a spectrum from robust to fragile epigenetic states. Interestingly, structural variants, common in subtelomeric sequences across eukaryotes, dictate local epigenetic stability. These findings reveal that subtelomeres, long recognized for their sequence variability, form a dynamic mosaic of coexisting epigenetic domains. This implies a wide range of gene-repressive regulatory logic at the chromosome ends, from environmental responsiveness to silencing stability.

papers.t: CREST functions as a molecular bridge between neuron-specific enhancers and epigenetic regulators in mature motor neurons.
papers.ab: Motor neuron development requires precise transcriptional regulation mediated in part by BAF (BRG1/BRM-associated factor) chromatin remodeling complexes. The neuron-specific BAF subunit CREST is critical for neuronal function and is mutated in some cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), yet its underlying genomic mechanisms remain unclear. Using mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation, we show that CREST is essential for motor neuron maturation by activating mature neuronal genes and repressing progenitor genes. Mechanistically, CREST interacts with the neuronal transcription factors ONECUT1 and NGN2, and the BRM ATPase to target pre-existing accessible enhancers of neuronal genes. CREST deletion selectively prevents CBP histone acetyltransferase recruitment, reducing histone H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers and downregulating target gene expression, without disrupting BRM binding, enhancer accessibility, or long-range chromatin architecture. Overall, our findings identify CREST as a crucial epigenetic mediator bridging lineage-specific transcription factors, BAF complexes, and CBP to activate enhancers and promote proper motor neuron development.

papers.t: Uhrf1 loss disrupts CTCF-associated chromatin organization during early mouse embryogenesis.
papers.ab: UHRF1 is a chromatin-binding protein essential for maintaining DNA methylation and histone modification states, yet its integrated role in vivo remains incompletely understood. To define its function, we generated conditional Uhrf1 knockout embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and embryos. Uhrf1⁻/⁻ ESCs exhibited near-complete loss of 5mC and 5hmC but maintained pluripotency, whereas Uhrf1-null embryos developed normally until E8.5 and then failed to develop further by E9.5, phenocopying Dnmt1 loss. Single-cell multi-omic (ME-seq) profiling of E8.5 embryos revealed impaired lineage stabilization, widespread hypomethylation, and disrupted chromatin architecture. Uhrf1 loss was associated with altered CTCF-associated chromatin signal, broad remodeling of chromatin contacts, altered cis-regulatory relationships, and reduced predicted BMP-related ligand-receptor communication, particularly within neural crest populations. These findings identify Uhrf1 as a central regulator that tightly couples DNA methylation maintenance to 3D genome organization during gastrulation, thereby, directing early lineage specification and positioning Uhrf1 as a pivotal mediator of epigenetic information transfer during early embryogenesis.

papers.t: IL-4 exploits TNF signaling to shape its gene expression signature in monocytes and macrophages.
papers.ab: Investigation of crosstalk between antagonistic pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines has focused on mechanisms and functional consequences of cross-inhibition. Here, we investigate cross-regulation between proinflammatory tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and anti-inflammatory interleukin-4 (IL-4) in primary human monocytes and in a skin wound-healing model. Surprisingly, TNF functioned mainly as a costimulator of IL-4-induced gene expression, whereas IL-4 selectively inhibited the TNF-induced IFN response, leaving inflammatory gene expression mostly intact. TNF and IL-4 synergistically induced gene sets that are important in the regulation of inflammation and tissue repair, which were highly induced during the phase of wound healing when these cytokines are co-expressed. Crosstalk between TNF and IL-4 was mediated by epigenetic chromatin-mediated mechanisms associated with cooperation between NF-κB and STAT6 transcription factors, erasure of negative histone mark H3K27me3, and selective inhibition of IRF1. These results identify a mechanism for expansion of the IL-4 response and highlight the complexity of crosstalk between antagonistic cytokines, including cooperation for select gene responses that are important for immune responses and tissue repair.

papers.t: Metabolically reprogrammed blastoids from totipotent-like stem cells exhibit enhanced tissue-specific organ-like development and placental formation.
papers.ab: While blastoids derived from pluripotent stem cells recapitulate pre- and early post-implantation embryogenesis, their long-term post-implantation development remains constrained. We define Snαnv, a chemical cocktail that promotes oxidative-phosphorylation-driven metabolic reprogramming, to efficiently generate ESC-blastoids with proper trophectoderm (TE)/inner cell mass (ICM) from conventional mouse ESCs at an efficiency of approximately 70%. These blastoids closely resemble blastocysts in morphology and cell-lineage allocation, with high Cdx2 expression in TE-like cells and notably display similar metabolic profiles. Furthermore, enhancing ESC totipotency via pladienolide B (PlaB) and crotonic acid (CA) augments the developmental potential of resulting PC-blastoids, which yield gonad-like tissues at E10.5, beating heart-like structures, and blood vessels under specific in vitro induction. These metabolically reprogrammed PC-blastoids are transcriptionally analogous to blastocysts by scRNA-seq. Moreover, they generate E7.0/E7.5-like embryos and placental structures comparable to E8.5 counterparts in vivo. Together, mimicking blastocyst metabolism and enhancing ESCs' totipotency yield blastoids with notably improved developmental competence.

papers.t: Transcription factor 3 cooperates with CXXC finger protein 1 to regulate histone H3K4 trimethylation and developmental competence in mouse oocytes.
papers.ab: During oogenesis, the establishment of oocyte-specific gene expression relies on epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling. Both histone modifications and transcription factors are crucial for the oocyte to acquire developmental competence; however, the mechanisms involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify transcription factor 3 (TCF3), an E-protein family member, as a key maternal regulator of oocyte developmental potential. Oocyte-specific deletion of Tcf3 results in female infertility, characterized by impaired meiotic maturation and early embryonic arrest at the two-cell stage. These defects are associated with defective maternal mRNA clearance and disrupted establishment of the H3K4me3 landscape in maturing oocytes. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that TCF3 directs H3K4me3 deposition at target gene promoters through interaction with CXXC finger protein 1 (CXXC1), the core subunit of the SETD1 histone methyltransferase complex. Importantly, this TCF3-CXXC1 interaction depends on their DNA-binding activity, highlighting the specificity of TCF3 in coordinating with CXXC1 to regulate maternal target genes, such as Pabpn1l. Together, our findings uncover a transcription factor-driven mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming that is essential for the maternal-to-zygotic transition.

papers.t: MethMarkerDB 2.0: an expanded and functionally annotated database for cancer DNA methylation biomarkers.
papers.ab: Cancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response, but their biological significance and potential applications remain to be systematically explored across datasets. To support this, we released MethMarkerDB 2.0 (https://methmarkerdb.hzau.edu.cn/v2), which provides several improvements over the previous version: (i) Expands the data resource from 13 to 21 cancer types and from 658 to 1236 whole-genome methylome samples, comprising ∼5.6 million candidate DMRs and 6411 literature-curated biomarker records.(ii) Integrates 450K DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Epigenome-Wide Association Study Atlas and transcript annotations into the "MethMarker Gene Search" module. These data provide complementary evidence from independent datasets and platforms and allow users to examine CpG-level information for individual DMRs. Additionally, cell-type-resolved reference methylation data allow users to check cellular-background methylation. (iii) Introduces four analysis modules to characterize DMR methylation patterns across age groups and spatial ecotypes, and connect DMRs with transcription factor binding evidence and cancer cell-line drug responses. Moreover, the "Methylation-Cas Designer" supports guide RNA design for methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme-Cas assays and targeted epigenome editing. In summary, MethMarkerDB 2.0 provides expanded resources, diverse functional analyses, and experimental design tools, facilitating the interpretation and application of cancer-associated DMRs.

papers.t: A RARγ-SMARCA5 chromatin-remodeling axis stabilizes AR luminal programs and opposes lineage plasticity in prostate cancer.
papers.ab: In prostate cancer (PCa), epigenomic mechanisms drive resistance to androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibitors, such as enzalutamide (enza). We tested whether retinoic acid receptor gamma (RARγ) shapes the epigenome to direct AR transcription, promote luminal identity, and limit enza resistance. RARγ restoration in enza-resistant 22Rv1 cells induced a large RARγ complex containing its coactivator TACC1 and the chromatin remodeler ISWI ATPase SMARCA5. RARγ restoration expanded and redistributed the AR cistrome toward active promoters, enhancers, and unique super-enhancers and increased the overlap with H3K27ac. RARγ restoration also increased SMARCA5 promoter-proximal binding that overlapped with G2/M-enriched AR cistrome, linking AR redistribution to cell cycle-associated chromatin engagement, including at luminal genes. In 22Rv1 and LNCaP C4-2 (also enza-resistant), RARγ restoration directed the AR transcriptome toward luminal differentiation. A miR-96 antagomir (targeting RARγ) mirrored the impact of RARγ restoration. RARγ antagonized the actions of the master lineage regulator ONECUT2 at the cistrome and transcriptome level and these antagonized genes were significantly associated with alternative lineages in murine PCa models of lineage plasticity and enza responsiveness and lineage plasticity in human PCa cohorts. These findings identify RARγ as a regulator of a chromatin remodeling mechanism that sustains luminal AR programs and opposes therapeutic resistance.

papers.t: PlantPAN 5.0: updated database for integrating multiomics evidence and exploring multilayered transcriptional regulatory networks in plants.
papers.ab: Plant Promoter Analysis Navigator (PlantPAN) 5.0 (https://plantpan.itps.ncku.edu.tw/) is an integrated multiomics resource for investigating plant cis-regulatory elements and transcriptional regulatory networks. This release expands genome annotations and promoter sequences to 240 species and provides 71 040 transcription factor (TF) annotations and 7762 nonredundant binding matrices. Its companion database, PCBase 3.0, substantially expands ChIP-seq data and newly incorporates ATAC-seq, bisulfite-sequencing, and four Hi-C-based chromatin interaction datasets for Arabidopsis thaliana. The new Differential Analysis function enables comparison of TF binding, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation across conditions. The redesigned Promoter Analysis interface provides TF family-level statistics, with a Pattern Overview panel integrating TF-binding site (TFBS) densities, plant DNA large language model-predicted open-chromatin regions, CpG-rich regions, and tandem repeats. Two new modules are introduced: (i) Transcriptome Regulatory Analysis and Coexpression, where candidate regulatory TFs and shared cis-elements in gene sets are prioritized through differential expression and coexpression analysis, and (ii) Interaction Topology Analysis for Chromatin and TFs, where chromatin interaction regions are integrated to reveal potentially coregulated genes and their shared TFs and predicted TFBSs. A Dockerized package enables large-scale local promoter analyses, with data privacy. Therefore, PlantPAN 5.0 is a comprehensive framework for discovering plant transcriptional regulatory mechanisms.

papers.t: KAS-CUT&Tag for direct mapping of transcription bubbles.
papers.ab: Transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) generates dynamic transcription bubbles as it moves forward, but existing methods map transcriptional activity indirectly. Here we introduce KAS-CUT&Tag, a method that combines N3-kethoxal labeling of exposed single-stranded DNA with CUT&Tag to directly map transcription bubbles. Bubble density correlates with nascent transcription levels and varies across Pol II-bound genes at promoters, gene bodies and termination regions. Transcription bubbles are enriched at genes marked by active histone modifications H3K27ac, H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 and by chromatin-bound splicing factor U2AF2, but enrichment is highest at replication-coupled histone genes in K562 and GM12878 cells. KAS-CUT&Tag also detects co-occupancy of the histone gene transcription factor NPAT with Pol II at the histone locus body, suggesting that in these cells NPAT is juxtaposed to transcription bubbles via interaction with Pol II. Together, KAS-CUT&Tag enables direct mapping of Pol II and regulatory interactions at transcription bubbles, providing a powerful tool for precise analysis of transcriptional activity.

papers.t: Single-nucleus multiomic profiling uncovers epigenetic dysregulation driving hippocampal vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.ab: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type-specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of human hippocampus to resolve gene regulatory architecture in AD. By linking chromatin accessibility to transcription, we identified more than 1000 disease-associated cis-regulatory interactions, highlighting coordinated epigenomic-transcriptomic remodeling. Excitatory cornu ammonis (EX.CA) neurons exhibited disproportionate regulatory disruption, characterized by increased chromatin accessibility coupled to activation of apoptosis-related gene programs, whereas dentate gyrus (EX.DG) neurons remained comparatively resistant. In glial cells, regulatory network inference revealed activation of transcription factor modules centered on SPI1/KLF4 in microglia and STAT3 in astrocytes, defining epigenetic programs that are highly associated with inflammatory and metabolic state transitions. Comparative evaluation with the prefrontal cortex uncovered conserved inflammatory activation alongside region-specific immune regulatory divergence, indicating spatially distinct microglial responses. Furthermore, cross-species integration demonstrated that a substantial fraction of AD-associated regulatory elements are human-specific, with AD-risk variants enriched in microglial cis-regulatory elements at loci including BIN1 and APOE. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking chromatin remodeling to cell-type-specific dysfunction and reveal human-specific regulatory architecture as a crucial factor to AD vulnerability and translational limitation.

papers.t: STAT3 controls IL-6-induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages.
papers.ab: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with selective STAT3 degradation, we show that STAT3 controls IL-6-induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages. Graded STAT3 chromatin recruitment scales with locus-specific H3K27ac deposition and transcriptional output across homeostatic and inflammatory programs. STAT3 degradation permits STAT1 recruitment at a subset of regulatory regions and engages a delayed amplification loop that is partially dependent on STING and type I IFN signaling. In severe COVID-19, monocytes exhibit exaggerated STAT3-associated inflammatory signatures together with attenuated STAT1-associated interferon responses, consistent with a skewed STAT3-STAT1 balance. These findings define a framework in which STAT3 calibrates IL-6-induced chromatin output while maintaining pathway fidelity by limiting STAT1 cross-talk.

papers.t: H3K9 demethylase KDM3A potentiates interferon signaling and macrophage-driven inflammation in atherosclerosis.
papers.ab: Macrophages drive atherosclerosis through inflammatory activation programs shaped by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. H3K9 methylation enforces heterochromatin states and represses transcription, whereas removal of this histone modification creates transcriptionally permissive chromatin. Here, we identified KDM3A-mediated H3K9 demethylation to enhance chromatin accessibility at interferon (IFN) signaling loci, thereby promoting IFN production and downstream IFN-dependent transcriptional and chemokine responses. In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, hematopoietic Kdm3a deficiency reduces lesion size, necrotic core formation, and neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, Kdm3a-deficient macrophages show impaired chemokine secretion and reduced neutrophil recruitment both in vitro and in vivo. In primary human macrophages, KDM3A knockdown suppressed IFN responses; consistently KDM3A-dependent gene signatures were enriched in IFN-inducible macrophages within human atherosclerotic plaques, and computational modeling predicted a shift toward more stable plaque phenotypes upon KDM3A inhibition. Together, these findings establish KDM3A as an epigenetic regulator that sustains IFN-driven macrophage activation and promotes progression of atherosclerosis, nominating KDM3A as a potential target for selectively modulating IFN-dependent inflammation.

papers.t: ZSCAN4 links a transient reset of repetitive DNA to genome integrity and cellular plasticity.
papers.ab: ZSCAN4 is transiently expressed in a small subset of embryonic stem cells and early embryos and has traditionally been linked to telomere elongation and genome stability. However, accumulating evidence indicates that ZSCAN4 does not function as a classical stemness factor. ZSCAN4 acts as a temporally restricted regulator of genome plasticity. Recent mechanistic studies indicate that ZSCAN4 preferentially operates at repetitive DNA regions. In particular, at telomeres, it supports maintenance and elongation, whereas, at microsatellite-rich and two-cell (2C)-associated loci, it has been proposed to enable a brief, locally restricted window of chromatin relaxation. This process involves noncanonical mechanisms, such as proteostasis-dependent removal of repressive chromatin complexes, coordinated engagement of genome surveillance pathways, and rapid restoration of chromatin constraint. ZSCAN4 activity is regulated by multilayered regulatory mechanisms acting at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and posttranslational levels, ensuring a sharp burst followed by active shutdown. We propose a unifying model in which ZSCAN4 functions as a transient genome reset factor that facilitates cellular plasticity during zygotic genome activation, 2C-like transitions, and cellular reprogramming, while preserving long-term genome integrity. This framework redefines the role of ZSCAN4 beyond stemness maintenance and highlights repetitive DNA as a central regulatory platform during developmental and reprogramming-associated genome transitions.

papers.t: How microbes reprogram immunity through epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation.
papers.ab: Microbial communities shape immunity through antigens, structural ligands, and metabolites, but how these transient signals are translated into stable, reversible, or disease-promoting immune cell states remains incompletely understood. This review examines epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation as interconnected layers of host-microbiota interactions. We discuss how microbial signals engage chromatin- and RNA-regulatory pathways across epithelial, myeloid, lymphoid, and stromal compartments, placing the microbiota-N6-methyladenosine (m6A) axis within the broader landscape of host and microbial RNA modifications. This framework helps explain how the same microbial molecule can promote barrier repair, immune tolerance, inflammation, or antitumor immunity depending on tissue exposure, responding cell type, and host state. We distinguish between association, microbiota dependence, and direct regulatory causality, and highlight knowledge gaps concerning non-m6A RNA modifications and bidirectional regulatory mechanisms. Finally, we outline key experimental and translational considerations, including microbial function, host target engagement, cell specificity, spatial delivery, and disease context. These insights highlight chromatin and RNA regulation as potential mechanistic links between microbial ecology and immune function that welcome further experimental investigation.

papers.t: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification.
papers.j: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
papers.ab: Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Using auditory neurons as an in vivo model, we investigate the role of the proneural factor NEUROD1 in regulating neuronal differentiation timing and subtype specification. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline Neurod1 deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse (Neurod1ST) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic Neurod1 expression. In the first phase, coinciding with Neurod1 upregulation during early neuronal differentiation, NEUROD1 preferentially binds putative enhancers of neuronal differentiation genes and promotes their transition to active chromatin states, consistent with pioneer factor activity. Loss of Neurod1 disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of Neurod1 in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors, Neurod1 deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.

papers.t: Acute degradation of Pumilio proteins reveals a biphasic posttranscriptional regulatory hierarchy in embryonic stem cell fate decision.
papers.j: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
papers.ab: Posttranscriptional regulation is critical for mammalian embryogenesis yet has been underexplored. We previously showed that RNA-binding Pumilio proteins (Pum1/2) are essential for early mouse embryogenesis and embryonic stem cell (ESC) functions. Here, using acute protein degradation systems combined with time-resolved RNA sequencing and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation, we delineate a two-phase regulatory hierarchy modulated by Pum1/2 in mouse ESCs. The first phase, occurring within 10 h of Pum1/2 depletion, is predominantly stabilization of over 100 Pum1/2-target mRNAs, while the second phase, occurring in subsequent 66 h, propagates to over 1,000 mRNAs mostly through indirect regulatory effects. Functionally, Pum1/2 depletion delays transition from naïve to formative pluripotency and alters expression trajectories of neuroectoderm and germline genes during early differentiation. Mechanistically, Pum1/2 directly repress mRNAs encoding Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 subunits, including Suz12, thereby potentially constraining H3K27me3 deposition at neuroectodermal gene loci. These findings establish Pum1/2 as biphasic posttranscriptional regulators of pluripotency and lineage balance.

papers.t: NANOG and OCT4 dosage shapes non-monotonic gene expression responses during stem cell differentiation.
papers.ab: Precise regulation of transcription factor (TF) expression is critical for maintaining cell identity, but studies on how graded expression levels affect cellular phenotypes are limited. To address this gap, we employed human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) as a dynamic model to study gene dosage effects and systematically titrated key TFs NANOG and OCT4 expression using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi). We then profiled transcriptomic changes in hESCs under self-renewal and definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation conditions using single-cell RNA-seq. Quantitative modeling of these Perturb-seq datasets uncovered distinct response patterns for different types of genes, including a striking non-monotonic up-regulation of on-target lineage genes during DE differentiation. This behavior extended to the ESC-to-neuroectoderm transition, suggesting non-monotonic responses of lineage genes to pluripotency regulator dosage are a recurring feature of lineage transitions. Together, these findings underscore the importance of characterizing TF function across a gradient of expression levels.

papers.t: PIWIL2 suppresses pluripotency in the male mouse germline.
papers.ab: Germ cells can give rise to teratomas and express pluripotency-associated genes, yet they remain intrinsically resistant to reprogramming by Yamanaka factors. The mechanisms governing this resistance are poorly understood. Here we identify PIWIL2 as a key suppressor of pluripotency in the male germline. While spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) normally lack SOX2 expression, Piwil2- but not Piwil4-deficient SSCs aberrantly express SOX2 and readily acquire pluripotency upon concurrent loss of Dmrt1 and Trp53. piRNAs associated with the Sox2 locus are detected in embryonic gonocytes but not in SSCs. Piwil2 deficiency reduces DNA methylation at the Sox2 promoter and increases DMRT1 and the RNA-binding protein DAZL, which jointly restrict Sox2 expression. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of PIWIL2 in repressing germline pluripotency and underscore the importance of coordinated transcriptional and translational regulation in maintaining germ cell identity.

papers.t: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma.
papers.ab: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. If and how tumor plasticity of EWS::FLI1-regulated transcriptional signatures contributes to disease progression is not known. To address this, we utilized a single-cell co-assay of RNA and chromatin accessibility (ATAC) sequencing to identify gene regulatory networks in EwS. By comprehensively characterizing regulatory elements across cell lines, we identified multiple unique modules of gene regulation. Differential usage and prevalence of these modules was evident across cell lines, associated with distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures, and in specific cases, modifiable by exogenous TGF-β. When we examined primary EwS patient tumors, we observed these same regulatory modules were variably enriched both across and within tumors, highlighting the existence of intratumoral heterogeneity in gene regulatory networks. Our findings demonstrate that multiple, co-existing transcriptional programs shape the phenotypic diversity of EwS and suggest that the balance between these networks may have important implications for clinical outcomes and targeted therapy development.

papers.t: Cis-regulation and natural selection in the evolution of human DNA methylation.
papers.ab: The vast collection of human-specific traits-such as our unique morphology, cognition, behavior, and diseases-has long been attributed to gene expression divergence between us and our closest living relatives, chimpanzees. Theory suggests that changes to cis-regulatory elements such as promoters and enhancers may drive evolutionary adaptation, and DNA methylation is a key factor in transcriptional cis-regulation. However, we still lack an understanding of (1) how species-specific methylation patterns arise; (2) their downstream effects; and (3) whether they are a common target of natural selection. In this study, we investigated these three questions. By combining a novel hypothesis testing framework with DNA methylation data from six human and chimpanzee cell types, as well as fused interspecies hybrid cells, we disentangled cis- vs. trans-acting methylation divergence across the genome. Across cell types, we found that methylation divergence is primarily driven in cis, which can be linked in some cases to nearby sequence variants such as CpG gains and losses. Although less common, regions with trans-acting methylation divergence were enriched for specific transcription factor (TF) binding motifs, suggesting a role of TFs such as FOXM1 in these differences. Having established these causes of methylation divergence, we then examined the functional consequences of differential methylation. Although methylation lacks a consistent relationship with transcription, we observed that associations between methylation and gene expression are stronger for genes with cis-regulatory divergence. Moreover, we identified lineage-specific selection shaping promoter methylation at the level of entire pathways, including those associated with human-specific traits such as speech, cognition, and susceptibility to infection with hepatitis C. Collectively, our findings provide a mechanistic framework suggesting that DNA methylation may occupy a key position, mediating the effects of both cis- and trans-acting factors on transcriptional networks, including those contributing to human-specific traits.

papers.t: Hypertranscription: the invisible hand in cancer epigenetics.
papers.ab: Global upregulation of transcription, or hypertranscription, is observed in most human cancers, driven by the action of oncogene-encoded transcription factors (TFs). TF interactions with RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) are mediated by kinases that phosphorylate the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) to drive productive elongation. The combinatorial complexity of hundreds of transcription factors and kinases acting on thousands of genes that differ in expression between cell types obscures common features that may result from hypertranscription. One of these features is histone overexpression, which can accelerate cell-cycle progression and cause transcription-replication conflicts, triggering chromosomal instability. Pol II profiling provides a direct measure of hypertranscription and histone gene upregulation in cancer, a pan-cancer diagnostic to stratify patient populations and follow the course of treatment. As many broadly effective anticancer drugs target Pol II activity, a better understanding of how they counteract hypertranscription has implications for drug development and for improved treatment regimens. Here we review the underlying mechanisms that drive hypertranscription and its impact on chromosome integrity, aging and neoplasia.

papers.t: Maternal diabetes causes embryonic cranial neural tube defects is associated with elevated H3K18cr and reduced AKT/PIKFYVE.
papers.ab: Neural tube defects (NTDs) are severe congenital malformations resulting from incomplete neural tube closure during embryogenesis, with maternal diabetes mellitus being a well-established risk factor. However, the underlying epigenetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we established a maternal diabetes mouse model by intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin at embryonic day (E) 5.5 and examined embryos during the critical neural tube closure period (E8.5-E10.5). Embryos from diabetic dams developed both cranial and spinal NTDs, with a marked predominance of cranial defects; we therefore focused our analyses on cranial neural tissues from affected embryos. In the cranial neural tissue of NTD-affected embryos, we observed significant accumulation of crotonyl-coenzyme A (Cro-CoA), accompanied by elevated levels of lysine crotonylation (Kcr) and histone H3 lysine 18 crotonylation (H3K18cr). Notably, maternal hyperglycemia-induced downregulation of HDAC1 and HDAC2, together with crotonyl-CoA accumulation, promoted a global increase in H3K18cr in cranial neural tissues. However, despite this global elevation, H3K18cr enrichment was paradoxically reduced at the promoters of AKT and PIKFYVE in cranial NTD embryos, correlating with their transcriptional silencing and contributing to cranial NTD pathogenesis. In HT-22 hippocampal neurons, exogenous glucose and crotonate recapitulated the metabolic and epigenetic alterations, leading to Cro-CoA accumulation and a global increase in H3K18cr. However, at the promoters of AKT and PIKFYVE, H3K18cr levels were decreased and consequently suppressed cell proliferation. Our findings demonstrate that maternal diabetes induces NTDs, at least in part, through aberrant elevation of H3K18cr, which suppresses the expression of AKT and PIKFYVE and impairs neural cell proliferation. Our findings reveal a potential regulatory mechanism by which abnormal H3K18cr elevation contributes to the occurrence of cranial NTDs induced by maternal diabetes.

papers.t: Defining the levels of the chromatin landscape using the I-CATCH system.
papers.ab: UNLABELLED: Alterations of the epigenome, including histone tail post-translational modifications (PTMs), have been shown to regulate the expression of genes important for driving multiple cellular processes including cellular differentiation, aging and tumorigenesis. Although the ability to measure histone tail PTM levels is integral to the understanding of chromatin biology, because of technological limitations, the proportion of nucleosomes that have histone tail PTMs at genomic loci remain undefined. To overcome this limitation, we developed the immuno-profiling of dCas9 targeted chromatin (I-CATCH) system, a technology designed to measure and normalize the levels of nucleosomes and co-occurring histone tail PTMs at targeted loci. Here, we show that the I-CATCH system has high analytical performance for measuring the levels of histone tail PTMs and we report the normalized levels of multiple histone tail PTMs at different genomic loci from both HeLa cells and human plasma. While further studies are required to determine the full utility of the I-CATCH system, we are hopeful that the I-CATCH system will help enable the ability to investigate new important features of chromatin biology. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65001-w.

papers.t: Peripheral DNA methylation of candidate Alzheimer's disease risk genes and its associations with cognition, brain volume and amyloid-β burden.
a: Australian Imaging Biomarkers and Lifestyle (AIBL) Study
papers.ab: UNLABELLED: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a growing major public health issue, affecting millions of people worldwide. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified over 50 loci associated with late-onset AD risk. However, most disease-associated variants are located in noncoding regions of the genome, making it difficult to elucidate exactly how disease risk is affected. Variants within noncoding regions can modulate disease risk through mechanisms such as gene expression regulation, which can be regulated by DNA methylation, which has, in recent years, been implicated in dementia and AD. This study utilised data from two well-characterised longitudinal studies, the Australian Imaging, Biomarker and Lifestyle (AIBL) study (n = 565) and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; n = 533), and aimed to investigate the association between peripheral blood DNA methylation at CpG sites located in previously implicated AD-risk genes and cognition, MRI volumetric measures and brain Aβ-amyloid (Aβ) burden. Analyses were undertaken across the preclinical to prodromal population as well as within subsets classified by clinical diagnosis and Aβ burden using two methods: all CpG sites within a candidate gene and a representative site from each gene region with the greatest variance (mean absolute deviation; MAD). We identified numerous associations in the AIBL cohort that remained significant after correction for the false discovery rate, although only one novel site was validated in the ADNI cohort. This was located within the gene body region of CR1 (cg00416522) and was associated with ventricle volume in cognitively unimpaired individuals with high brain Aβ burden. While this study's results contribute to a growing literature that supports the role of epigenetic modifications in ageing and AD-related traits, they suggest that there are limited associations of peripheral DNA methylation with cognitive and neuroimaging traits in the a priori AD-risk genes that were screened in this study. Future meta-analyses across studies with larger cohort sizes and phenotypically rich datasets will help to confirm this finding and potentially elucidate further associations, while unbiased approaches are warranted and may uncover novel peripheral DNA methylation associations. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-64935-5.

papers.t: Interplay between epigenetic alterations and piRNA expression in cancer development.
papers.ab: PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs generated from longer precursor transcripts through primary processing and, in selected biological contexts, a secondary ping-pong amplification cycle. They associate with PIWI proteins to target and silence transposable elements (TEs), and dysregulation of the PIWI-piRNA pathway has been reported in multiple human cancers. In physiological germline models, epigenetic modifications - including DNA methylation, histone modifications, RNA modifications, and chromatin remodeling - coordinately regulate the activity of piRNA clusters to ensure proper piRNA biogenesis. However, in tumor cells, how epigenetic modifications influence piRNA transcription and processing remains poorly characterized, with most studies focusing on how dysregulated piRNAs drive tumorigenesis via epigenetic or epitranscriptomic mechanisms. This review also discusses species-specific differences, limitations in somatic piRNA annotation, and the evidence needed to distinguish association from mechanism. DNMT/HDAC inhibitors, dietary bioactive compounds, and deactivated Cas9 (dCas9)-based epigenome editing may provide useful experimental or therapeutic approaches, but piRNA-directed epigenetic therapy remains preclinical.

papers.t: Intermittent reduced-dose methotrexate enabled continuation of induction therapy despite severe delayed methotrexate elimination in primary central nervous system lymphoma: a case report.
papers.ab: BACKGROUND: High-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) is the backbone of induction therapy for primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) but may be limited by delayed elimination and renal toxicity. We report a clinically instructive case in which intermittent reduced-dose methotrexate allowed continuation of induction therapy after severe delayed elimination and acute kidney injury. CASE PRESENTATION: A 59-year-old Japanese woman presented with headache and rapidly progressive impaired consciousness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 5-cm enhancing mass in the right frontal lobe with significant perifocal edema. Emergent open biopsy confirmed PCNSL, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, non-germinal center B-cell type, without systemic involvement. Induction chemotherapy with rituximab, methotrexate, procarbazine, and vincristine was initiated. After the first HD-MTX dose (3.5 g/m2), methotrexate elimination was markedly delayed (72-h level 0.85 µmol/L; persistent elevation around day 7), accompanied by a > 60% reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate from 79.2 to 29.4 mL/min/1.73 m2. Because of renal dysfunction, subsequent courses employed an intermittent reduced-dose methotrexate strategy (1.2 g/m2 on selected cycles). With this approach, serum methotrexate concentrations remained within an acceptable therapeutic range without recurrent delayed elimination, and renal function gradually improved. Complete remission was achieved after induction, followed by consolidation with reduced-dose whole-brain radiotherapy and two courses of high-dose cytarabine. Complete remission has been maintained for 30 months after completion of the entire treatment sequence. CONCLUSIONS: When severe delayed methotrexate elimination and renal dysfunction occur early during HD-MTX-based induction for PCNSL, an intermittent reduced-dose strategy may allow continuation of methotrexate-based therapy and subsequent standard consolidation in selected settings. This case also highlights the practical importance of supportive care and individualized decision-making when glucarpidase is not readily available.

papers.t: Evolutionary lineage-specific and heterochromatin-independent repression of transposon-derived sequences.
papers.ab: At least one-quarter of our gene regulatory sequences are derived from transposable elements (TEs). Their rapid evolutionary turnover fuels the innovation of species-specific regulatory networks, yet their activity must be tightly controlled for the integrity of broader gene regulatory programs. Although this is in part achieved through heterochromatin-based repression, notably by KRAB domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs) in tetrapods, the regulatory landscape of TEs remains to be fully characterized. Here, we discover that SCAN domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (SZFPs), which originally arose through capture of the sequence encoding a retroviral capsid by a KZFP gene, have expanded their gene repertoires and diversified their DNA recognition specificity in a lineage-specific manner across amniotes. Our comprehensive identification of human SZFP binding sites revealed that they bind regulatory elements derived from distinct TE subfamilies of matching evolutionary ages. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that SZFP binding sites are inaccessible nucleosome-associated chromatin without accompanying heterochromatin marks, H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, and resist opening by pioneer transcription factors such as SOX2 and POU5F1 (also known as OCT4) as well as SWI/SNF-mediated gain of an enhancer-associated chromatin state. These results unravel a rapidly evolving epigenetic machinery responsible for controlling lineage-specific TE-derived regulatory sequences in a heterochromatin-independent fashion.

papers.t: Tumor-intrinsic PTPN12 suppresses anti-tumor immunity in colorectal cancer by restraining a dual epigenetic and cytoskeletal dsRNA sensing program.
papers.ab: Innate sensing of endogenous double-stranded RNA and the ensuing interferon response are crucial for the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibition. Microsatellite stable colorectal cancer characteristically lacks this response, remaining immune-refractory with undefined intrinsic regulators. Here, through an in vivo clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats screen, we identify PTPN12 as a physiological barrier that suppresses double-stranded RNA sensing and interferon response. TRIM28 was identified as a direct PTPN12 substrate here; PTPN12 removes phosphorylation at Y370 to stabilize repressive complexes and silence transposable elements, while concurrently rewiring the adhesive cytoskeleton to disrupt the spatially organization of cytosolic double-stranded RNA required for efficient innate sensing. Pharmacological inducible PTPN12 knockdown inhibits pre-established tumor growth and overcomes immunotherapy resistance in vivo, recapitulating PTPN12 ablation-induced massive double-stranded RNA accumulation. Our findings reveal a role for PTPN12 in coupling epigenetic silencing with cytoskeletal surveillance, suggesting potential strategies to augment anti-tumor immunity and overcome immunotherapy resistance in microsatellite stable colorectal cancer.

papers.t: Circulating chromatin reveals effects of disease-associated variants on gene regulation.
papers.ab: A fundamental challenge in human genetics is determining how regulatory genetic variation shapes complex traits and disease risk. Chromatin quantitative trait loci can link disease-associated variants to regulatory element activity, but mapping them in disease-relevant tissues at scale remains challenging. We leverage epigenomic liquid biopsy by profiling histone modifications in circulating chromatin from 328 cancer patients and 38 healthy individuals to identify cell-free chromatin quantitative trait loci.
